A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViLLa and VideoReasonSeg, with identifiable correspondence between their methods and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, although revised datasets and protocols prevent some direct score comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark results and component ablations in Tables 1–7, plus an aggregation-strategy experiment in Appendix C.

after.justification: V3 reports original benchmark comparisons, component and sampling ablations, a direct-adaptation control, and a qualitative failure analysis in its main text and appendices.

M1.justification: V3 adds a Grounded-VideoLLM-based Key Segment Extractor that identifies query-relevant intervals and combines global and neighboring reference frames before encoding. This substantially changes video processing. The Context Synthesizer and Hierarchical Temporal Synchronizer largely rename v1's context aggregation module and video-frame decoder, retaining their equations and training objectives.

E1.justification: VideoReasonSeg adds MovieChat and VideoMME sources and explicitly includes long videos exceeding five minutes, extending its temporal and scene coverage. V3 also evaluates MeViS and ReVOS. Ref-YouTube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS17, and the existing VIS benchmarks remain, with VIS evaluation relocated to the appendix.

E2.justification: VideoReasonSeg comparisons remove Mask2Former, VITA, and PixelLM rows and add LMPM, OnlineRefer, VideoLISA, and VISA; LISA configurations change from Llama/Llama2 to LLaVA. The retained referring benchmarks gain URVOS, LBDT, DsHmp, VideoLISA, and VISA comparisons. Appendix A additionally evaluates the direct-adaptation baseline ViLLa†.

E3.justification: VideoReasonSeg changes from 1,934 samples split 1,000/400/534 into train/validation/test to 3,000 videos split 2,000/1,000 into training/validation, with short/long reporting. Segmentation evaluation switches from AP/AR to J&F. New sampling experiments vary reference-frame counts over 0, 6, and 12. The stated core training budget remains unchanged.

E4.justification: The three-row component ablation becomes an eight-configuration study of three modules. V3 adds direct-adaptation and sampling-strategy controls, reference-frame sensitivity, and a temporal-localization failure case. The helmet comparison against LISA/PixelLM is replaced by an occluded-sheep comparison against VISA. The earlier aggregation-strategy study is retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; additional ablation configurations do not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V3 replaces VideoReasonSeg results under its revised dataset and metric and adds MeViS and ReVOS results, including ViLLa J&F scores of 49.4 and 57.0. Reported Ref-DAVIS17 J&F changes from 64.4 to 74.3, while VIS AP changes from 67.1/59.5/46.2 to 67.6/59.9/46.5. These are revised reported results, not controlled same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The task and token definitions, attention and decoder equations (1)–(5), momentum assumption, and training losses retain their mathematical substance. V1's loss equation becomes inline text. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the standard J&F explanation adds no new mathematical result.

C1.justification: V1 claims to introduce video reasoning segmentation and its first model. V3 acknowledges existing VRS approaches and reframes its contribution around overcoming their limitations in long, crowded, rapidly moving, and occluded videos through three modules. Its benchmark contribution also expands to 3,000 videos and 15,000 object descriptions.

C2.justification: V3 introduces explanations involving key-frame error propagation, sampling redundancy, and single-token limitations, and argues against simple static-model adaptation in Appendix A. Appendix E attributes a bystander-selection failure to missing a late-occurring talking action. V1's explicit text-only-input and no-multiround-conversation limitations disappear, without evidence that those restrictions were resolved.

D1.justification: Core hardware, optimizer, loss weights, and training hyperparameters remain essentially unchanged. V3 specifies the extractor implementation and one-third global/two-thirds neighboring-frame sampling, and documents GPT-4V without v1's additional Qwen-VL attribution. It removes the promised code/dataset repository link; this changes access information without establishing actual resource availability.

R1.justification: V3 substantially repositions ViLLa relative to VISA and VideoLISA, discussing their limitations instead of claiming the first VRS solution. It also adds relevant work including Grounded-VideoLLM, GLaMM, and OMG-LLaVA. This changes the closest-prior-work narrative, beyond citation or publication-metadata updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V1's duplicated Related Works sections are consolidated; task, method, and benchmark material is reorganized under Section 3 with separate module subsections. Terminology changes throughout, and the appendix is reorganized to accommodate discussion and failure analysis.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column presentation. The architecture diagram and introductory examples are substantially redrawn, the qualitative comparison is replaced, and new data and failure examples appear. Tables gain short/long/overall groupings, additional benchmarks, and expanded controls. VIS results move to the appendix; the existing data-generation figures are retained.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation through relevant video-reasoning competitors, fuller component ablations, direct-adaptation and sampling controls, and explicit failure analysis. These address v1's limited comparison coverage and component attribution; removing duplicated related work also improves clarity. The omitted release link and limitations are drawbacks, and Table 1 contains an inconsistency: OnlineRefer's overall score is below both subgroup scores. These defects temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in evidence and explanation.
